newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.Africa money market discounting Bank rate hike.
newsitem.headline: S.Africa money market discounting Bank rate hike.

text.p: South African money market rates kicked up on Wednesday as a high money market shortage kept a tight grip on liquidity.

Traders said the rise in short-term rates signalled the market was discounting a hike in the key Bank rate -- currently at 16 percent -- and the present tight situation was likely to remain until early 1997, with Christmas spending looming.
But despite the squeeze market players were not convinced Reserve Bank Governor Chris Stals would move yet, rather preferring to hold his hand on Bank rate for the time being.
Three-month rates rose to 16.75 percent offered from 16.40 percent on Tuesday as the 90-day Bankers' Acceptance rate moved to between 16.25 and 16.10 percent from 15.90 to 15.75 percent previously.
The Reserve Bank indicated the shortage at 9.379 billion rand on Tuesday from 9.265 billion rand on Monday.
"With the shortage remaining high and call rates remaining around the 16.75 level, the banks had to move their BA rates otherwise they would be lending money out at a loss," a senior dealer said.
He said that the rise in BA and call rates to over 16 percent also signalled that the market was discounting a Bank rate hike.

"Effectively banks can go to the Reserve Bank with liquid assets and raise funds at 16 pct, but they are paying their clients 16.75 pct," he said. "We definitely should have had a rate hike over the last little while."
Failing an interest rate hike, the dealer said the market would need an inflow of capital from offshore to loosen the squeeze on liquidity.
Another senior trader felt, however, that the central bank would be loathe to raise rates, primarily because higher interest rate in the past had failed to attract inflows.
He said that the Bank Governor Chris Stals was also likely to be content with keeping the squeeze on banks as part of the central bank's efforts to rein in burgeoning credit demand.
"I don't think (Stals) has much sympathy with the banks...maybe he still thinks that the banks are to blame for the high shortages with their credit extension," the trader said.
Credit extension to the private sector in September was running at 355.37 billion rand from 349.4 billion rand in August and up 17.94 percent from a year ago.
And figures released by the National Association of Automobile Manufacturers of South Africa on Tuesday indicated that a slowdown in credit demand was unlikely in the near future, economists said.
Car sales in October were at their highest in 14 years, which economists said showed consumer spending was not slowing and would place further upward pressure on demand for credit.
The trader also said that he expected the shortage to remain high until deep into January as the Christmas spending period got underway.
"We expect very high shortages until January as notes and coins usually go up over the Christmas period...there will be pressure on liquidity," he said.
The shortage was expected to average at about nine billion rand and notes and coins between 20 to 22 billion rand, he added.
Notes and coin liability stood at 19.43 billion rand on Tuesday from 19.525 billion rand on Monday.
